lesson.title: Formatting Strings with .format(): From Placeholders to Polished Output
lesson.summary: The .format() method lets you build a string as a template with placeholders, then fill those placeholders with values, giving you precise control over spacing, decimal places, and order.
lesson.body:
Concatenating strings with the + operator gets ugly fast, especially once numbers enter the picture. Try to build the sentence "Score: 87.5%" by gluing pieces together and you run into a wall: the number 87.5 is a float, not a string, so Python refuses to add it directly to text. You end up wrapping every value in str(), and the code becomes a tangle of plus signs that is hard to read and easy to break. The format method solves this by letting you write the sentence as a template first, with placeholders marked by curly braces, and then filling those placeholders in with a separate list of values.

The basic pattern is "template".format(value1, value2, ...). Each pair of empty braces {} in the template is replaced, in order, by the next argument passed to format. For example, "{} scored {}%".format("Maria", 87.5) produces the string 'Maria scored 87.5%'. You can also number the braces explicitly, like {0} and {1}, which lets you reuse a value more than once or place it out of order: "{1} beat {0}".format("Sam", "Tia") produces 'Tia beat Sam', because {1} refers to the second argument, at index 1, and {0} to the first.

Where format really earns its keep is in controlling how numbers look. Inside the braces you can add a colon followed by a format specification. "{:.2f}".format(3.14159) produces '3.14', rounding to two decimal places. "{:5d}".format(42) produces '   42', padding the integer to a width of five characters. "{:,}".format(1000000) produces '1,000,000', inserting comma separators automatically. These specifications build directly on the idea of string formatting you already know: you are still turning values into readable text, but now you have a precise, declarative way to say how many digits, how much padding, and what separators to use, instead of computing that formatting by hand with slicing and concatenation.

Keyword arguments make longer templates far easier to follow. Instead of counting positions, you can write "{name} is {age} years old".format(name="Ken", age=16), which produces 'Ken is 16 years old'. This is especially valuable once a template has four or five placeholders, since matching numbered braces to a long argument list invites mistakes, while named placeholders read almost like plain English and stay correct even if you reorder the arguments later.

It helps to trace through a realistic case. Suppose you compute an average with average = sum(scores) / len(scores) and get 91.33333333333333. Printing that raw number looks unprofessional. Writing print("Average: {:.1f}".format(average)) rounds and formats in one step, producing 'Average: 91.3'. The template stays fixed while the value changes, which is exactly the point of the method: you separate what the output should look like from what the actual data is, so the same formatting code works no matter what numbers flow through it.
